title: Photosynthesis and chemosynthesis
summary: How does light energy become food, and how do producers that get no light survive?
cards.0.h: Photosynthesis: the equation and why it matters
cards.0.p: Plants, algae and cyanobacteria use light energy to make glucose from CO₂ and water. Along the way, O₂ is released. In this way, light energy becomes chemical bond energy.
cards.0.svg#4: light energy → chemical bond energy in glucose
cards.0.key: Chlorophyll captures the light. The energy of food chains, the O₂ in the air and fossil fuels are all products of photosynthesis.
cards.1.p: The chloroplast is an organelle with a double membrane. The flat sacs inside it are called thylakoids, and their stacks are called grana. Chlorophyll is found in the thylakoid membrane. The fluid around the thylakoids is called the stroma, and the Calvin cycle takes place there.
cards.1.key: The plural of granum is grana. Cyanobacteria have no chloroplasts. Their chlorophyll is in thylakoid membranes inside the cell.
cards.1.etk.soru: Tap the parts of the chloroplast.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.0.acik: The chloroplast has a double membrane. The membranes control what goes in and out.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.1.acik: A granum is a stack of thylakoids piled on top of each other. The plural is grana, and the grana are linked to each other by stroma thylakoids.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.2.acik: A thylakoid is a flat sac. Its membrane holds chlorophyll, and the light-dependent reactions happen here.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.3.acik: The stroma is the fluid around the thylakoids. Here the Calvin cycle turns CO<sub>2</sub> into glucose.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.4.acik: The chloroplast has its own circular DNA. It makes some of its proteins itself.
cards.1.etk.noktalar.5.acik: The chloroplast's own ribosomes make proteins from the genes in its own DNA.
cards.1.once.soru: Does the chloroplast have its own DNA?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: The stroma contains its own DNA and ribosomes. It makes some of its proteins itself.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: DNA is not found only in the nucleus. Chloroplasts and mitochondria have it too.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The chloroplast has both DNA and ribosomes.
cards.2.p: Chlorophyll a is the main pigment, found in the reaction center. Chlorophyll b and carotenoids capture light of other colors and pass the energy on to chlorophyll a.
cards.2.svg#16: Mg at the center of chlorophyll
cards.2.key: The carotenoids are orange carotene and yellow xanthophyll, and they also protect the plant from too much light. Accessory pigments widen the range of light that is captured.
cards.2.once.soru: Why do leaves turn yellow in autumn?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: When chlorophyll breaks down, the yellow and orange carotenoids that were in the leaf all along become visible.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.yazi: A new yellow pigment is made
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The yellow pigments are in the leaf in summer too, but chlorophyll hides them.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: Drying comes later. The color change starts when chlorophyll breaks down.
cards.3.p: An absorption spectrum shows how much of each color a pigment absorbs. Chlorophyll absorbs blue-violet and red light and reflects green light. An action spectrum shows how fast photosynthesis goes in different colors.
cards.3.key: A leaf looks green because it reflects green. The absorption spectrum measures the pigment, the action spectrum measures photosynthesis and the two overlap.
cards.4.h: Early experiments: where does the mass come from?
cards.4.p: Van Helmont grew a willow tree for five years with only water. The tree gained about 74 kg, but the soil hardly decreased at all. Van Helmont thought the mass came from the water, because he had not taken the air into account.
cards.4.svg#16: most of the dry mass comes from CO₂ in the air
cards.4.key: In the 1770s, Priestley and Ingenhousz showed that a plant restores air spoiled by a candle only in light. Most of a plant's dry mass comes from the CO₂ in the air.
cards.5.p: The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membrane. Chlorophyll excited by light loses electrons, and the photolysis of water replaces them. Along the way, O₂ is released. This stage produces ATP and NADPH.
cards.5.key: H⁺ ions build up inside the thylakoid, and ATP is made as they flow back to the stroma through ATP synthase. The electrons finally pass to NADP⁺. If water containing ¹⁸O is given, labeled O₂ is released.
cards.5.once.soru: Why is water split in the light-dependent stage?
cards.5.once.secenekler.0.neden: Chlorophyll excited by light loses electrons, and the photolysis of water replaces them. O₂ is a by-product.
cards.5.once.secenekler.1.neden: Glucose is made in the Calvin cycle in the stroma.
cards.5.once.secenekler.2.neden: CO₂ binds to RuBP in the Calvin cycle. It does not combine with water.
cards.6.p: Light is captured by photosystem II and photosystem I. Noncyclic electron flow produces ATP, NADPH and O₂. In cyclic flow, only photosystem I works, and only ATP is made.
cards.6.key: The reaction center of photosystem II is P680, and that of photosystem I is P700. In noncyclic flow, electrons go from water to PS II, through the chain to PS I, then to NADP⁺. Cyclic flow makes no O₂ and no NADPH.
cards.6.once.soru: In some light reactions, an electron returns to the same photosystem without involving water at all. Is O₂ released along this path?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Water is not split, so no O₂ is released. Only ATP is made.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: O₂ is released only when water is split. This path does not use water.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Water is not used, so no O₂ is released at all.
cards.7.p: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma. CO₂ is attached to 5-carbon RuBP by the enzyme rubisco. The PGA that forms is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH. Most of the PGAL is used to remake RuBP.
cards.7.key: The remaining PGAL goes to making glucose. One glucose uses 6 CO₂, 18 ATP and 12 NADPH. The cycle does not use light directly, but it depends on light. In the dark, it stops once the ATP and NADPH run out.
cards.8.p: As light intensity and the amount of CO₂ increase, the rate of photosynthesis first rises, then levels off. The rate is highest at the optimum temperature. At higher temperatures, enzymes break down. The rate is low in green light.
cards.8.key: The temperature curve is bell-shaped, while the light and CO₂ curves level off. The rate of photosynthesis is high in blue-violet and red light.
cards.9.p: The rate of photosynthesis is set by the scarcest factor. On the flat part of the graph, adding more light does not help, but adding CO₂ raises the curve. When water runs short, the stomata close and CO₂ intake drops.
cards.9.svg#4: on the flat part, more light
cards.9.key: Mg and N are part of the structure of chlorophyll. When they are lacking, leaves turn yellow. The amounts of chlorophyll and enzymes, the number of stomata and the leaf's structure are internal factors that also affect the rate.
cards.10.p: Some bacteria and archaea do not use light. Instead, they oxidize inorganic substances and use the energy released to make organic matter from CO₂. This is called chemosynthesis.
cards.10.svg#1: NH₃, NO₂⁻, H₂S, Fe²⁺ are oxidized
cards.10.key: Nitrifying bacteria enrich the soil by turning ammonia into nitrite and nitrite into nitrate. Chemosynthesis is found only in prokaryotes, and it produces no O₂.
cards.10.once.soru: At deep-sea vents that get no light at all, who starts the food chain?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: These bacteria get energy by oxidizing substances such as H₂S and make food from CO₂.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Mosses need light, and there is no light there.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The area around the vents is full of worms, mussels and crabs.
cards.11.p: In hot, dry weather, the stomata close and photosynthesis becomes less efficient. C4 plants first hold CO₂ in a 4-carbon compound. CAM plants open their stomata at night and store CO₂.
cards.11.key: When the stomata close, rubisco starts binding O₂. This is called photorespiration. In C4 plants, CO₂ is concentrated in the cells that run the Calvin cycle. In CAM plants, CO₂ stored at night enters the Calvin cycle during the day.
cards.11.once.soru: When does a cactus open its stomata?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: If a cactus opened its stomata during the day, it would lose a lot of water. So it takes in CO₂ at night and stores it.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: In the desert, stomata left open during the day lose a lot of water.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: The stomata have to open for the plant to take in CO₂.
cards.12.p:
• Glucose is made from CO₂ and water using light energy. The O₂ released comes from water.
• In the thylakoid, light energy produces ATP, NADPH and O₂.
• The Calvin cycle in the stroma uses these to turn CO₂ into glucose.
• The scarcest factor limits the rate.
• In chemosynthesis, the energy comes from oxidizing inorganic substances.
quiz.0.q: Group each event by the stage of photosynthesis it happens in.
quiz.0.e: In the light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid, water is split, O₂ is released and ATP and NADPH are made. The Calvin cycle in the stroma attaches CO₂ to RuBP, reduces PGA to PGAL using ATP and NADPH and regenerates RuBP.
quiz.1.q: How many ATP are used in the Calvin cycle to make 3 glucose?
quiz.1.e: One glucose uses 18 ATP. So 3 glucose need 3 × 18 = 54 ATP.
quiz.2.q: Sort each feature into photosynthesis, chemosynthesis or both.
quiz.2.e: In photosynthesis, the energy comes from light and water is split. In chemosynthesis, the energy comes from oxidizing inorganic substances. Nitrifying bacteria are an example. In both, the producer makes organic matter from CO₂.
quiz.3.q: A plant was given CO₂ whose oxygen was labeled with ¹⁸O. Where does the labeled oxygen show up?
quiz.3.o.1: In the O₂ released and in glucose
quiz.3.o.2: Only in the water that reacts
quiz.3.o.3: In glucose and in the water formed
quiz.3.e: The O₂ released comes from the photolysis of water. The oxygen of CO₂ goes into glucose and into the water formed at the end of the reaction.
quiz.3.y.0: The O₂ released comes from splitting water. The oxygen of CO₂ goes into glucose and the water formed.
quiz.3.y.1: O₂ comes from the photolysis of water, not from CO₂. The labeled oxygen is found in glucose and in the water formed.
quiz.3.y.2: The oxygen of CO₂ does not go into the water that reacts. In the Calvin cycle, it goes into glucose and the water formed.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Trace the source of oxygen, find chlorophyll's colors, turn off the light and look for the limiting factor.
A:adimlar.0.baslik: Where does the oxygen come from?
A:adimlar.0.metin: In photosynthesis, CO₂ and water turn into glucose using light energy, and O₂ is released. We labeled the oxygen of the water with ¹⁸O and showed it in red. Play and follow the atoms.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Where do the oxygen atoms in the released O₂ come from?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The oxygen of CO₂ does not go into O₂.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: In the light-dependent stage, water is split and O₂ is released. This is called photolysis. That is why labeled water gives labeled O₂.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: Half from CO₂, half from water
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: All of the labeled oxygen showed up in O₂. None of the oxygen from CO₂ went into O₂.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Chlorophyll does not absorb every color equally. Change the wavelength and find the curve's second peak, in the red.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: Red light is at the right end of the spectrum, above 650 nm.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: The curve has two peaks: blue-violet and red. The green in between (about 550 nm) is the color absorbed least.
A:adimlar.2.metin: In the 1880s, Engelmann lit a filament-shaped green alga with light passed through a prism. Next to it he placed oxygen-seeking (aerobic) bacteria. These bacteria gather where a lot of O₂ is being made.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Where do the most bacteria gather?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Green is the color absorbed least. Photosynthesis and O₂ production are lowest there.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The rate of photosynthesis changes with wavelength. So O₂ is not made in the same amount in every region.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Most O₂ is made in these colors. This experiment showed how the rate of photosynthesis changes with wavelength, which is the action spectrum.
A:adimlar.3.metin: The Calvin cycle uses the ATP and NADPH made in the light stage to turn CO₂ into sugar. With the light on, the cycle keeps turning. Turn off the light and play.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: When the light went off, no new ATP and NADPH came. Once the supply ran out, the Calvin cycle stopped too.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A water plant gives off O₂ bubbles as it carries out photosynthesis. Change the light, CO₂ and temperature. The bubbles and the graph change right away. Find the following yourself.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.0.yazi: With CO₂ at 30%, increase the light. At what point does the rate stop rising?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.0.tamam: Once the light passed 30%, the rate did not rise, because CO₂ is now the scarcest factor. On the flat part of the graph, adding more light does not help.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.1.yazi: Make photosynthesis go as fast as possible.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.1.tamam: Light and CO₂ are enough, and the temperature is at the optimum (about 30 °C), so no factor is limiting the rate. At any moment, the scarcest factor sets the rate.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.2.yazi: With photosynthesis at its fastest, raise the temperature above 40 °C.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.bulgular.2.tamam: The rate dropped even though light and CO₂ were plentiful. The Calvin cycle runs on enzymes, and enzymes break down at temperatures above the optimum.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The Calvin cycle runs on enzymes. Count the bubbles the water plant gives off and set the temperature to the value where photosynthesis is fastest.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: Raise the temperature step by step. When the bubbles start to drop, go back one step.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: The rate of photosynthesis is highest at the optimum temperature. At higher temperatures, enzymes break down and the rate falls quickly.
A:kapanis.0: The O₂ released in photosynthesis comes from water.
A:kapanis.1: Chlorophyll absorbs blue-violet and red light and reflects green light.
A:kapanis.2: The light-dependent stage makes ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle stops when they run out.
A:kapanis.3: The rate of photosynthesis is limited by the scarcest factor. This factor can be light, CO₂ or temperature.
A:kapanis.4: The temperature curve is bell-shaped. At very high temperatures, enzymes break down.
